description: Mamy team składający się z 4 osób. Wszyscy wspólnie studiujemy Space Tech na AGH w Krakowie. Wykruszyły się nam dwie osoby więc szukamy ewentualnie kogoś chętnego do współpracy z zakresu AI oraz grafiki do uzupełnienia naszego TEAMU :)
summary:
OASIS (Outpost for Antarctic Simulation of Interplanetary Settlements) proposes the Bunger Hills Oasis in East Antarctica (66°15′S 100°45′E) as an Earth analog for permanent bases at the lunar south pole and in Jezero Crater on Mars. Bunger Hills is one of Antarctica’s largest ice-free areas (~950 km²): bare frost-shattered rock, fresh and saline lakes, extreme cold, katabatic winds and about 350 km of isolation from the nearest operating station. Yet it is far less studied than better-known analogs such as the McMurdo Dry Valleys.

We built an interactive web map that shows Bunger Hills, the lunar south pole and Jezero Crater side by side using NASA GIBS, Moon Trek and Mars Trek data. It includes an honest 8-factor analog score (Moon 38 %, Mars 43 %) that also shows what Antarctica cannot reproduce. Around the existing A. B. Dobrowolski Station we designed a modular, autonomous outpost deployed over five field seasons (power, communications, hub, ELF/Schumann science, robotics and regolith 3D printing). It tests, year-round, the technologies a Moon or Mars base will need before they leave Earth.
details:
What it does
OASIS answers the challenge “Identify Earth Locations that Analog the Permanent Moon Base Locations and Mars” with one specific, under-used site: the Bunger Hills Oasis in East Antarctica. It has two parts: a research report that compares Bunger Hills with the lunar south pole and Jezero Crater across eight themes (caves, geology, terrain, temperature, water, dust, biology, logistics), and the interactive OASIS Analog Map that makes this comparison visible and checkable.

How it works

  • Three linked maps. Earth: NASA GIBS (MODIS Terra true colour, MODIS land-surface temperature, ASTER GDEM relief) plus a high-resolution Esri basemap. Moon: LRO WAC imagery and LRO LOLA elevation from NASA Moon Trek, re-projected in the browser to a south-polar view, with a contrast control for the dark polar terrain. Mars: Viking MDIM 2.1 and MGS MOLA from NASA Mars Trek.
  • MODIS date picker with “Find clear day”: it checks every day within ±15 days of the chosen date, skips missing-data and polar-night images, and picks the least cloudy one.
  • Download image: saves the current Bunger Hills view as a PNG with a scale bar, the data layer, the date and the credits.
  • Analog score: 8 factors (temperature, terrain, surface material, water & ice, sunlight cycle, isolation & logistics, atmosphere, gravity & radiation), each scored 0–5 for the Moon and Mars, with sources. Totals: Moon 38 %, Mars 43 %. The strongest match for both is isolation & logistics. Factors Antarctica cannot reproduce (vacuum, low gravity, radiation) are scored 0 on purpose, so the score stays honest.
  • OASIS outpost: five modules placed around the existing Polish A. B. Dobrowolski Station, in deployment order: (1) power source, (2) communications, (3) hub module with crew shelter for service visits, (4) ELF/Schumann science, (5) robotics & 3D printing from regolith simulants.

Benefits
Bunger Hills combines low Sun angles and long shadows (like the lunar south pole), frost-shattered rock, cold and dust (like Mars), ancient-lake analogs studied in NASA-linked work, and real isolation with only one field season per year. That makes it a place to test GNSS-free navigation, power systems for the dark season, cold-resistant mechanics, dust protection and remote, autonomous operations, with the same “no one around to fix it” constraint as a lunar or Martian base. The outpost is deployed one module per season over about five years. Every module keeps running through the following winters, so each season builds on a core that has already proven itself. Reusing an existing station keeps the cost and the environmental footprint low.

What we hope to achieve
We want Bunger Hills to be recognised and used as a dedicated Moon–Mars analog site. The first step is a real deployment of the OASIS core modules at the A. B. Dobrowolski Station, run with the station’s operators and the Polish polar community. From there, OASIS would grow into a long-term, remotely operated test bed that agencies, universities and companies can use to qualify hardware before it flies. The analog score and map are open source, so the same method can be reused to assess other candidate analog sites.

Tools, languages and software
HTML, CSS and JavaScript in a single file; Leaflet for the Earth and Mars maps; OpenLayers + proj4js for the lunar polar projection; hosted on GitHub Pages. No installation or account is needed. Source code: https://github.com/Eminiction/oasis-analog-map

What makes it creative
Instead of a generic similarity ranking, we picked one little-known site and built an honest, transparent comparison: every score has a source, and the factors Earth cannot reproduce are shown, not hidden. The map puts three worlds next to each other with live NASA data, and the outpost concept turns the analog into a concrete, staged test programme.

Factors we considered
Scientific fit (geology, temperature, water, dust, illumination), logistics and access (one season a year, about 350 km to the nearest operating station), environmental protection of the oasis, reuse of existing infrastructure, power through the dark months, communications, and the limits of any Earth analog (atmosphere, gravity, radiation).

Team: AGH Space Tech Team – Izabela Świca, Piotr Libudzki, Mikołaj Głód, Michał Para
